title: VB9-08749
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX (the Appellant). He is a citizen of Montenegro and alleges that he is gay. He alleges that he was the victim of violence and discrimination due to his sexual orientation and that the police did not assist him when he requested assistance. He fled to Canada and claimed refugee status.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected his refugee claim. It made the following main conclusions: a. He testified that his first fell in love with a man in 2007 but in his basis of claim (BOC) form, he first never mentioned this. In an amended BOC he stated that this took place three years later in 2010; b. He testified that he asked police for help on three occasions but in both versions of his BOC he states he never asked the police for assistance; c. The Appellant provided no corroborative evidence of his sexual orientation; d. State protection is adequate in Montenegro and the Appellant's own allegations of seeking police assistance are not credible.

The Appellant has appealed this decision and is now asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to recognize him as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, he asks that this matter be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. While the Appellant requests to submit new evidence, no new evidence is contained in his Appellant's record. He also requests an oral hearing. His main arguments are as follows: a. The RPD erroneously expected the Appellant to prove his sexuality through evidence of a same-sex relationship b. The RPD failed to consider the Appellant's background when considering his involvement with the LGBT community and his same-sex activity; c. The RPD failed to consider which gender or sexual orientation category the Appellant fell into and this could have impacted its credibility and state protection analysis; d. The Appellant did not mention when he first fell in love with another man in his original BOC because he thought he only had to describe the problems he faced; e. The RPD breached procedural fairness by requiring the Appellant to conduct his hearing via videoconference.
In rendering this decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE guidelines).

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection. I accept, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is a gay man. However, I find that the Appellant has not established that he ever reached out to the police for protection. I further find that the Montenegrin authorities would be able to protect him adequately as a gay man if he were to return.

The Appellant requests an oral hearing. According to the case law, the RAD must determine whether the requirements for an oral hearing set out in subsection 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) have been met.1 One of the determining factors is that new evidence presented on appeal must have been found to be admissible. The Appellant has not submitted any new evidence. As there is no new evidence to be analyzed in a hearing before the RAD,2 the request is denied.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3 There is no breach of procedural fairness that resulted from conducting the RPD hearing via videoconference

The Appellant argues that the RPD breached procedural fairness by requiring the Appellant to conduct the hearing via videoconference. I disagree. Videoconferencing is an accepted technology that generally respects the principles of procedural fairness.4 I have reviewed the hearing which was conducted respectfully and gave the Appellant ample opportunity to present oral evidence, make representations and know the case to be met. I find that there was no breach in procedural fairness resulting from the fact that the hearing was conducted via videoconference. State protection: the law

In order to be granted refugee status, a claimant must demonstrate through clear and convincing evidence that the state in their country of origin is unable to protect them adequately. Claimants are generally required to demonstrate that they made reasonable efforts to seek state protection. For the reasons that follow, I find that the Appellant did not make reasonable efforts to seek state protection and that the Montenegrin state offers him adequate protection as a gay man. The Appellant has not established that he approached the police for assistance

The RPD found that the Appellant did not reasonably explain why he did not mention his attempts at seeking state protection in either his original or his amended BOC. The Appellant did not contest this finding and I agree with it. I find that the Appellant has not established that he sought assistance from the police.

In the Appellant's original BOC, he was directly asked if he had sought protection or assistance from any authorities including the police and he said he did not because he knew the police would not help him.5 In his amended BOC, he repeated that he never asked the police for help for similar reasons.6 However, in his hearing he testifies to asking the police for help on three occasions and that they refused to help him.

I agree with the RPD that the Appellant explanation for this inconsistency, that the interpreter must have made a mistake, is not reasonable. He signed the original BOC, stating that it was complete true and accurate. He also had an opportunity to provide this information in his amended BOC but instead, he repeated his answer that he did not seek help from the police as they would not help him. I also note that he stated in a Port of Entry interview that he did not seek police assistance.7

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant never sought protection or assistance from the police or any other authorities in relation to incidents or violence involving his sexual orientation. The country documentation on LGBT individuals in Montenegro

The country documentation relating to the treatment of LGBT individuals in Montenegro is mixed. LGBT individuals face discrimination and harassment from the population.8 Some public LGBT activists and figures have faced violence.9 That being said, there is an increasing trend towards greater visibility of LGBT individuals in everyday life, every police station has an officer dedicated to serving this population and NGOs are working with the police to foster better communication and trust between LGBT individuals and the police.10 A decision to ban a pride parade was overturned by the Constitutional Court and there were multiple examples of the police efficiently and effectively arresting and charging perpetrators of violent attacks against LGBT individuals.11 The Ombudsman's Office received and investigated a number of complaints from LGBT individuals and reported a drop in the number of complaints. In 2016, the Office only received three complaints of discrimination based on sexual orientation.12

I note that one report submitted by the Appellant before the RPD states that institutions and authorities are incapable of protecting the rights of LGBT people in Montenegro,13 but this report is from 2012 and I place less weight on it than on the more recent reports cited above. I prefer the more recent articles because many improvements in protecting LGBT individuals have taken place in the last ten years in Montenegro.

While there are still areas for improvement in terms of protections for LGBT individuals in Montenegro, I find that there is adequate state protection for the Appellant in his specific circumstances. I note that he was never a public figure or activist and has never stated that he has this ambition. The Appellant's arrest and conditional sentence do not establish mistreatment by the police

The Appellant alleged that he was involved in a fight with a group of young men who were bad-mouthing him because he is gay. He alleges that the incident led to him being charged and receiving a conditional sentence because the police hate gay people. He did not seek police assistance, but they got involved as the fight got worse.

The RPD noted in the hearing that the Appellant mentioned that he defended himself with a broken bottle which may have led to him being charged and sentenced. The Appellant conceded this as a relevant factor and the RPD concluded that his arrest and sentencing was due to him using a bottle as a weapon rather than due to any discrimination or harassment from the police related to his sexual orientation. I agree. The Appellant did not contest this conclusion.

While the Appellant states that he was arrested and sentenced because he was gay, he acknowledged that he used the bottle as a weapon and that this might have influenced the result. I also note that there is no evidence of discrimination or mistreatment of LGBT individuals by the police force and the justice system in the patterns of charging and sentencing in the country documentation. The Appellant has also provided no evidence to corroborate his version of this incident. Given the country documentation, the Appellant's own concession and the lack of any evidence to show otherwise, I find that this incident does not represent an example of harassment or discrimination by authorities against the Appellant. I have credibility concerns discussed above in relation to the Appellant's contradictory testimony about his interactions with authorities and find that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. This credibility issue has also been relevant in reaching my conclusion as to this interaction with the police as they involve similar allegations. The Appellant did not make reasonable efforts to seek state protection

In coming to my conclusion as to whether there is adequate state protection for the Appellant, I am to consider if he made reasonable efforts to seek state protection. I find that he did not. As discussed above, he has not established that he ever sought state protection.

It is clear from the country documentation that authorities have made great strides in offering operationally effective protection to LGBT individuals. I find that protection would be reasonably forthcoming for the Appellant if he were to seek state protection. While discrimination and harassment from the general population does persist, it is not reasonable that the Appellant did not even try to seek protection from state authorities who have demonstrated that they take incidents of discrimination, harassment and violence against LGBT individuals seriously. Adequate state protection exists for the Appellant in Montenegro

In conclusion, there is adequate state protection in Montenegro for the Appellant who identifies as gay. For this reason, he is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection. Other arguments and conclusions not determinative

The Appellant argues without merit that the RPD failed to determine his specific gender identity or sexual orientation. The Appellant identifies himself specifically as a gay man in his BOC and his amended BOC and this identity was confirmed by the RPD at the hearing. There is no basis to the argument that his specific identity was not canvassed and identified correctly by the RPD.

The Appellant argues that the RPD was overly focused on his same-sex relationships and his involvement in the gay community in determining whether he was gay. The RPD does appear to have expected corroborative evidence of the Appellant's sexual orientation through support letters from ex-partners and community groups without analysing his explanations for not having this evidence. I agree with the Appellant that this is an error under the SOGIE guidelines.14 However, I have focused on state protection in this decision and have accepted that the Appellant is gay on a balance of probabilities, so this error is not determinative of this appeal.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection.
